lesson.topicTitle: Structure and functions in living organisms

specAnchors.text: understand that the central nervous system consists of the brain and spinal cord and is linked to sense organs by nerves
understand that stimulation of receptors in the sense organs sends electrical impulses along nerves into and out of the central nervous system, resulting in rapid responses

primer.text: You already know that sense organs detect changes around you. This note maps the wiring that turns detection into action: the brain and spinal cord at the centre, nerves radiating outward, and electrical impulses sprinting along neurones. Learn the pathway vocabulary here — it repeats in every reflex and sense-organ question later in the course.

modules.title: Structure of the nervous system
modules.opening: The nervous system splits into a central part — the brain and spinal cord — and a peripheral part of nerves reaching every corner of the body. Information travels as fast electrical impulses along cells called neurones, and a nerve is simply a bundle of those neurones. The central section processes incoming signals and coordinates the reply.
keyPoints: The central nervous system is the brain plus the spinal cord.
The peripheral nervous system is every nerve branching from the centre to the rest of the body.
Neurones carry electrical impulses; a nerve is a bundle of neurones.
Nerves reach the sense organs, letting the brain communicate with all body regions.

low.restatement: Two divisions: the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord) does the processing, and peripheral nerves carry messages to and from it.
low.analogy: Think of a headquarters with roads leading to every town — the headquarters decides, the roads deliver.
low.examPointer: Spell out the CNS abbreviation on first use: examiners want 'central nervous system — brain and spinal cord' as the full phrase.

medium.restatement: Electrical impulses along neurones give the system its speed; bundled neurones form nerves that link the central coordinating centre to sense organs and effectors.
medium.analogy: Nerves are broadband cables made of many wires (neurones), so losing one wire rarely cuts the whole connection.
medium.examPointer: Questions award the mark for 'bundle of neurones' — do not call a nerve a single cell.

modules.title: Function: receptors, impulses and rapid responses
modules.opening: Detection starts when receptors in a sense organ are stimulated — by light, sound, touch, temperature or chemicals. The receptors fire electrical impulses that race along sensory neurones into the central nervous system, which replies through motor neurones to effectors. Because the signal is electrical, the whole loop runs in a fraction of a second.
keyPoints: Receptors in sense organs detect stimuli such as light, sound, touch, temperature and chemicals.
Sensory neurones carry those impulses into the central nervous system.
Motor neurones carry instructions out to effectors — muscles that contract or glands that secrete.
The relay from receptor through sensory neurone and CNS, then motor neurone to effector, produces a rapid response.

low.restatement: A stimulus fires receptors; impulses flow in along sensory neurones, the CNS decides, and motor neurones instruct effectors to respond.
low.analogy: It is a call centre: the hotline (sensory) brings the complaint in, the operator decides, the dispatch line (motor) sends the fix.
low.examPointer: Practise writing the full pathway in order — sequence marks are lost when a step is skipped.

medium.restatement: The pathway runs in one direction per arc: input neurones enter the centre, output neurones leave it, and the electrical medium makes the round trip nearly instantaneous.
medium.analogy: Like a roundabout with one-way lanes — inbound traffic never mixes with outbound, so nothing slows the loop.
medium.examPointer: Do not write 'nerves think' — award language is 'CNS processes the information and coordinates the response'.

glossary.definition: The brain and spinal cord together — the coordinating centre of the nervous system.
A specialised cell that carries electrical impulses; bundled neurones form nerves.
A neurone carrying impulses from receptors in the sense organs into the central nervous system.
A neurone carrying impulses from the central nervous system out to effectors.
